title: Vada Pav, Misal Pav and a Full Bar: An Indian Family Is Betting Columbus Wants the Real Mumbai Experience
excerpt: Bombay House Restaurant & Bar opens this month in the former Winking Lizard space near Polaris, bringing pan-Indian flavors and handcrafted Indian-inspired cocktails to central Ohio.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Bombay House offers a pan-Indian menu, unlike typical American Indian restaurants.
  • The restaurant features Mumbai street food like vada pav and misal pav.
  • Columbus's Indian population is growing, driven by tech and education sectors.
  • Bombay House includes a full bar with Indian-inspired cocktails.
  • The restaurant aims to redefine Indian dining for the Indian diaspora in America.

The Columbus Dispatch
There is a moment every NRI knows. You walk into an Indian restaurant in an American suburb, scan the menu and find the usual suspects — butter chicken, chicken tikka masala, garlic naan, maybe a saag paneer. The food is fine. It is also not what anyone in India would recognise as a complete picture of Indian dining. The Kondhare family in Columbus, Ohio is betting that moment is over. ## Bombay House: Pan-India in the Midwest Bombay House Restaurant & Bar is set to open this month at 496 Polaris Parkway, taking over part of the space left vacant when the Winking Lizard — an Ohio chain known for beer and wings — closed in 2023. The concept is deliberately ambitious: a pan-India menu that spans the entire subcontinent, paired with a full bar serving Indian-inspired cocktails. "Our goal is to create a complete dining experience where both the food and drinks celebrate the richness and diversity of Indian cuisine," the Kondhare family told The Columbus Dispatch. What makes Bombay House different from the Indian restaurants already in Columbus is its refusal to pick a lane. Most Indian restaurants in mid-sized American cities specialise — they are North Indian, or they are South Indian, or they focus on a specific regional cuisine. The Kondhares have hired chefs from different Indian regions, each bringing their own expertise, to create a menu that reflects the country's staggering culinary breadth. ## The Street Food Bet The dishes the family is most excited about are not from the tandoori-and-tikka canon at all. They are from the streets of Mumbai. **Vada pav** — the city's iconic street sandwich, a crispy potato fritter seasoned with spices and tucked into a soft toasted bun with house-made chutneys — leads the charge. It is the food that fuels Mumbai's 20 million residents, sold for roughly 20 rupees at thousands of street stalls. In Columbus, it will be plated in an upscale setting with ingredients sourced from around the world. Then there is **misal pav**, a fiery slow-cooked sprouted bean curry from Maharashtra, layered with crispy farsan, fresh onions, coriander and lemon, served with bread rolls. And **pav bhaji**, the late-night street-food classic of slow-simmered vegetables mashed with butter and spices, served with buttered rolls. These are dishes that rarely appear on Indian restaurant menus outside cities with large Maharashtrian populations. Their presence on the Bombay House menu is a statement: the Kondhares are cooking for people who know Indian food, not just people curious about it. ## A Growing Trend: Indian Dining Goes Everywhere Columbus is not an obvious destination for ambitious Indian dining, but the Kondhares are not alone in seeing opportunity beyond the coastal metros. In Longmont, Colorado, Sheel Joshi — a chef with 44 years of experience and a nod from Michelin's 2009 guide for his Beverly Hills restaurants — is opening a small Indian kitchen this summer. In Fort Collins, Bawarchi is expanding to a second location. Khan Saab, the first Michelin-recognised Pakistani restaurant in Southern California, is opening in Santa Monica this month. The U.S. Census Bureau's 2020 data showed the Indian-American population at 4.8 million and growing fast, with some of the strongest growth in Midwest and Sun Belt cities. Columbus's Indian population has expanded significantly, driven by the tech sector and Ohio State University. Restaurants like Bombay House are following that population.
Street Food Staples on the Menu
›Vada Pav: Iconic Mumbai street sandwich.
›Misal Pav: Fiery sprouted bean curry.
›Pav Bhaji: Classic mashed vegetable dish.
›Focus on authentic regional dishes rarely found in U.S.
## The Cocktail Factor One element that sets Bombay House apart is its full bar program. Indian restaurants in the United States have historically underinvested in beverages, defaulting to the mango lassi and the Kingfisher. The Kondhares are building a cocktail menu from scratch, using fresh ingredients, premium spirits and house-made syrups and infusions inspired by Indian flavors. "Guests can expect creative drinks made with fresh ingredients, premium spirits and house-made syrups and infusions, alongside beer, wine and refreshing non-alcoholic beverages," the family said. Think cocktails infused with cardamom, tamarind, kokum and rose — the same ingredients that define Indian cooking, translated into the glass. ## What It Means for NRIs For the Indian diaspora in Columbus and across the Midwest, Bombay House represents a shift that has been years in the making. The generation of Indian-Americans now in their thirties and forties grew up watching their parents' cuisine reduced to a handful of dishes that white America deemed acceptable. They want the full spectrum — the heat of misal, the crunch of vada pav, the messy joy of pav bhaji eaten with hands. The Kondhares are not just opening a restaurant. They are making a bet that America is ready for the India their customers actually grew up eating.
Cocktails with an Indian Twist
›Full bar program with Indian-inspired cocktails.
›Fresh ingredients and premium spirits used.
›Unique flavors: cardamom, tamarind, kokum, rose.
›Aiming to elevate beverage offerings in Indian dining.
## What's Next Bombay House Restaurant & Bar opens this month. Early indications suggest strong interest from Columbus's food community, with the restaurant positioned as a rare destination for authentic pan-Indian dining in central Ohio. If the concept works, it could become a model for ambitious Indian restaurants in mid-sized American cities — proof that great Indian food does not require a New York postcode or a six-figure build-out.
